tasks.title: Introduction
tasks.subtitle: History, setup, who created Python & first program
tasks.overview: Python is a modern, high-level programming language designed for readability and clarity. Discover who created Python, how it executes your instructions, and write your first functioning program.

lesson.heading: Who Created Python?
lesson.body: Python was created by Dutch programmer Guido van Rossum in the late 1980s at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands. Its initial release arrived in 1991. Van Rossum named the language after the British comedy troupe Monty Python's Flying Circus because he wanted programming to be engaging and enjoyable.

lesson.heading: The Core Philosophy & The Zen of Python
lesson.body: Unlike older languages that required complex boilerplate, Python follows the principle that 'Readability counts' and 'Simple is better than complex'. Python uses clean indentation rather than brackets to structure code, making it read almost like plain English.

lesson.heading: How Python Runs Your Code
lesson.body: Python is an interpreted language. When you run a script, the Python virtual machine compiles your plain text instructions into internal bytecode (.pyc) and executes it line by line from top to bottom.

lesson.heading: Your First Program
lesson.body: The built-in print() function tells Python to output text to standard output. String literals are enclosed in matching double or single quotation marks inside the parentheses.

examples.title: Your first print instruction
examples.code: print("Hello, Python!")
examples.explanation: print displays whatever expression is passed inside its parentheses. The quotes tell Python this is a string literal.

examples.title: Multiple output lines
examples.code:
print("Welcome to Easy Python!")
print("Built for developers.")
examples.output:
Welcome to Easy Python!
Built for developers.
examples.explanation: Python executes instructions in sequence from top to bottom. Each print call produces a new line by default.

practicals.prompt: Which instruction displays a message in Python?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! print() is Python's built-in function to display text or values to the terminal.

practicals.prompt: Was Python created by Guido van Rossum in the late 1980s?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! Guido van Rossum conceived Python in December 1989 and published version 0.9.0 in 1991.

practicals.prompt: Write one line that displays the text Ready to learn!
practicals.aiExplanation: Nice work! You used print("Ready to learn!") with proper parentheses and quotes.

tasks.title: Variables, Data Types, Input/Output
tasks.subtitle: Storing values, types (int, float, str, bool), input() & f-strings
tasks.overview: Programs store and manipulate data. Learn how Python variables name values in memory, explore fundamental data types, receive user input from the keyboard, and format text output.

lesson.heading: Variables as Named Labels
lesson.body: In Python, a variable is not an empty box; it is a label bound to an object in memory (Hunt's object model). Writing score = 10 creates the integer 10 in memory and points the name 'score' to it. Variable names must start with a letter or underscore and are case-sensitive.

lesson.heading: Core Built-In Types
lesson.body:
Python has four foundational scalar data types:
- int: Whole numbers (e.g. 42, -5)
- float: Decimal numbers (e.g. 3.1415, 0.5)
- str: Text characters inside quotes (e.g. 'hello', "Python")
- bool: Logical truth values (True or False)

lesson.heading: Dynamic Typing & type()
lesson.body: Python is dynamically typed. You do not declare variable types explicitly; Python determines the type automatically at runtime based on the value assigned. Use type(x) to inspect any object's type.

lesson.heading: Reading User Input
lesson.body: The input(prompt) function pauses program execution, waits for the user to type in the terminal, and always returns the input as a string (str). When you need numbers for math, convert them using int() or float().

lesson.heading: Modern Output with f-strings
lesson.body: Formatted string literals (f-strings) let you embed expressions directly inside text by prefixing the string with 'f' and enclosing variable names in curly braces {}. For example: f"Hello, {user_name}!".

examples.title: Assigning variables and using f-strings
examples.code:
user = "Maya"
age = 22
print(f"{user} is {age} years old.")
examples.explanation: The f prefix evaluates the expressions inside {user} and {age} and interpolates them cleanly.

examples.title: Converting string input to integer
examples.code:
entry = "15"
count = int(entry)
print(count + 5)
examples.explanation: int("15") transforms the text '15' into the numeric integer 15 so mathematical addition can occur.

practicals.prompt: What does a .py file usually contain?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Files ending in .py are Python source files containing plain text code.

practicals.prompt: In a few words, what should you check after running a program?
practicals.aiExplanation: Exactly! Checking program output lets you verify that your code behaved as intended.

practicals.prompt: Display Start on one line and Finished on the next.
practicals.aiExplanation: Well done! You output two sequential lines using print('Start') and print('Finished').

tasks.title: Operators and Conditions (if/elif/else)
tasks.subtitle: Arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic & branching decisions
tasks.overview: Computers make decisions based on logical conditions. Master Python's arithmetic operators, comparison checks (==, !=, <, >), logical chaining (and, or, not), and if/elif/else branching.

lesson.heading: Arithmetic Operators
lesson.body:
Python provides full mathematical calculation capability:
+ (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (true division yielding float), // (floor division yielding integer), % (modulus/remainder), and ** (exponentiation).

lesson.heading: Comparison Operators
lesson.body:
Comparisons evaluate expressions and produce a bool (True or False):
- ==: equal to
- !=: not equal to
- <: less than, >: greater than
- <=: less than or equal, >=: greater than or equal
Caution: Do not confuse assignment (=) with equality comparison (==).

lesson.heading: Combining Decisions with and, or, not
lesson.body: Chain logic with keywords: 'and' requires both conditions to be True; 'or' requires at least one condition to be True; 'not' inverts the truth value.

lesson.heading: Branching with if, elif, and else
lesson.body: Python uses indentation (typically 4 spaces) to define blocks of code under an if statement. Python tests the if condition; if False, it checks successive elif clauses in order, and falls back to else if none matched.

examples.title: Branching based on temperature
examples.explanation: 28 is not > 30, but it is >= 20, so the elif branch runs and execution skips the else.

examples.title: Combining conditions with and
examples.code:
has_id = True
age = 19
if age >= 18 and has_id:
    print("Entry permitted")
examples.explanation: Both conditions evaluate to True, satisfying the and operator.

practicals.prompt: Does Python use curly braces {} instead of indentation to mark an if code block?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Unlike C or Java, Python uses whitespace indentation to define code blocks.

practicals.prompt: You need to check if a student score is between 80 and 100 inclusive. Which expression is correct?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! The 'and' keyword ensures both boundary checks must evaluate to True.

practicals.prompt: Write code that checks if x = 12 is greater than 10. If so, print "Greater".
practicals.aiExplanation: Great job! if x > 10: with an indented print("Greater") is the canonical syntax.

tasks.title: Loops (for, while)
tasks.subtitle: Iteration, sequences, range(), break & continue
tasks.overview: Repetition is the backbone of computing. Learn how for loops iterate over ranges and sequences, how while loops repeat until a condition changes, and how break and continue control loop flow.

lesson.heading: The for Loop and Iteration
lesson.body: A for loop in Python iterates directly over items in any sequence (list, string, range). Instead of tracking index counters manually, Python extracts each item into your loop variable: for item in collection:.

lesson.heading: Generating Numbers with range()
lesson.body: range(start, stop, step) generates an arithmetic progression of integers. The stop value is exclusive: range(1, 5) produces 1, 2, 3, 4. If start is omitted, it defaults to 0.

lesson.heading: The while Loop
lesson.body: A while loop repeats its indented block as long as its condition remains True. You must ensure the loop state updates toward false inside the body, otherwise you create an infinite loop.

lesson.heading: Loop Control: break and continue
lesson.body:
- break: Immediately terminates the loop and moves to the statement following it.
- continue: Skips the remainder of the current iteration and jumps to the next turn.

examples.title: Counting with range in a for loop
examples.code:
for n in range(1, 4):
    print(f"Step {n}")
examples.explanation: range(1, 4) produces values 1, 2, and 3. The loop runs 3 times.

examples.title: Countdown with a while loop
examples.code:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Lift off!")
examples.explanation: Each iteration decrements count by 1 until count reaches 0, ending the loop.

practicals.prompt: Does range(1, 5) include the number 5 in its output?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! The stop parameter in range() is always exclusive, so it stops at 4.

practicals.prompt: Which statement immediately halts and exits the enclosing loop?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! 'break' jumps completely out of the nearest enclosing loop.

practicals.prompt: Use a for loop and range(1, 4) to print each number on its own line.
practicals.aiExplanation: Excellent! for i in range(1, 4): print(i) outputs 1, 2, and 3.

tasks.title: Strings
tasks.subtitle: Indexing, slicing, immutability, formatting & string methods
tasks.overview: Strings are sequences of text characters. Understand zero-based indexing, slicing substrings with stride, string immutability, and essential built-in transformation methods like strip(), split(), and replace().

lesson.heading: Indexing and Slicing
lesson.body: Strings are zero-indexed: text[0] accesses the first character. Negative indices count backward from the end: text[-1] is the last character. Use slicing text[start:stop:step] to extract substrings. Reversing a string is cleanly expressed as text[::-1].

lesson.heading: Strings are Immutable
lesson.body: In Python, strings cannot be altered in place. Attempting text[0] = 'H' raises a TypeError. Every string transformation method produces and returns a brand-new string object.

lesson.heading: Essential String Methods
lesson.body:
- .upper() and .lower(): convert case
- .strip(): remove leading and trailing whitespace
- .replace(old, new): replace occurrences
- .split(delimiter): break text into a list of words
- delimiter.join(list): join items back into a single string

examples.title: Slicing and case transformation
examples.code:
banner = "python programming"
print(banner[:6].upper())
examples.explanation: banner[:6] slices the first 6 characters ('python'), and .upper() transforms it to uppercase.

examples.title: Splitting and joining
examples.code:
words = ["learn", "python", "now"]
print("-".join(words))
examples.explanation: join stitches list items together with the '-' hyphen separator.

practicals.prompt: Can you change an individual character in a Python string directly using s[0] = 'X'?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Strings in Python are immutable; you must construct a new string.

practicals.prompt: What method removes surrounding spaces from '  clean code  '?
practicals.aiExplanation: That's it! In Python, .strip() strips leading and trailing whitespace.

practicals.prompt: Extract and print the first 4 characters of word = "Developer".
practicals.aiExplanation: Awesome! word[:4] extracts the substring from index 0 up to 4.

tasks.title: Lists, Tuples, Sets, Dictionaries
tasks.subtitle: Data collections: mutable lists, immutable tuples, unique sets & key-value dicts
tasks.overview: Organize data using Python's four major built-in collections. Discover when to use mutable lists, fixed tuples, deduplicated sets, and high-performance key-value dictionaries.

lesson.heading: Lists: Ordered and Mutable
lesson.body: Lists are enclosed in square brackets: [1, 2, 3]. They are ordered, allow duplicates, and are mutable. You can add elements with .append(), remove elements with .pop() or .remove(), and modify elements in place: fruits[0] = 'mango'.

lesson.heading: Tuples: Ordered and Immutable
lesson.body: Tuples use parentheses: (10, 20). Like lists, they preserve order and allow duplicates, but once created, their elements cannot be changed or reassigned. Use tuples for fixed data records.

lesson.heading: Sets: Unordered and Unique
lesson.body: Sets are created with curly braces: {'apple', 'banana'}. Sets automatically eliminate duplicate entries and provide fast membership testing (item in my_set) and set math (union, intersection).

lesson.heading: Dictionaries: Key-Value Pairs
lesson.body: Dictionaries associate unique keys with values: student = {'name': 'Asha', 'grade': 'A'}. You look up values by key: student['name'] or safely with student.get('name'). Dictionaries are optimized for instant lookups.

examples.title: List manipulation
examples.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
fruits.append("cherry")
print(len(fruits))
print(fruits[1])
examples.explanation: append adds cherry to the end, making length 3. Index 1 accesses the second item, banana.

examples.title: Dictionary key-value access
examples.code:
book = {"title": "Python Guide", "pages": 280}
print(book["title"])
examples.explanation: Accessing the key 'title' returns its paired value 'Python Guide'.

practicals.prompt: Scenario: Turn these three fruits: apple, banana, cherry into a Python list.
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Square brackets [] define a mutable list in Python.

practicals.prompt: Can a Python set contain duplicate values?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! Sets automatically enforce uniqueness and discard duplicates.

practicals.prompt: Create a dictionary person with key "role" set to "Developer", then print person["role"].
practicals.aiExplanation: Great job! person = {"role": "Developer"} followed by print(person["role"]) retrieves the value.

tasks.title: Functions
tasks.subtitle: Modular code, def, parameters, return values & scope
tasks.overview: Functions allow you to package logic into reusable, modular blocks. Learn how to define functions with def, pass positional and keyword arguments, return calculation results, and understand variable scope.

lesson.heading: Why Functions Matter
lesson.body: Instead of duplicating code, functions encapsulate a task under a descriptive name. Functions make programs maintainable, testable, and easier to understand.

lesson.heading: Defining Functions with def
lesson.body: Define a function using the 'def' keyword followed by the function name, parentheses for parameters, and a colon: def compute_total(price, tax):. The indented block contains the function body.

lesson.heading: Parameters, Arguments & Default Values
lesson.body: Parameters are variable names in the function definition; arguments are the actual values supplied when calling it. You can supply default parameter values: def greet(name, greeting='Hello'):.

lesson.heading: Returning Values vs Printing
lesson.body: The return keyword passes a result back to the caller so it can be stored in a variable or used in further calculations. If a function reaches the end without a return statement, it implicitly returns None.

lesson.heading: Variable Scope (Local vs Global)
lesson.body: Variables created inside a function are local to that function and cease to exist once the function finishes executing. Global variables defined outside can be read from inside functions.

examples.title: A function that calculates and returns an amount
examples.explanation: add_tax computes the tax and returns 55.0 to the caller, which is formatted and displayed.

examples.title: Greeting function with default parameter
examples.explanation: The default value 'Engineer' is used because no second argument was provided.

practicals.prompt: Does a Python function without an explicit return statement return None?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! If no return statement is executed, Python functions implicitly return None.

practicals.prompt: Which keyword is used to declare a function in Python?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! 'def' stands for define and introduces a function in Python.

practicals.prompt: Define a function square(n) that returns n * n. Call square(4) and print the result.
practicals.aiExplanation: Great job! def square(n): return n * n correctly computes and returns 16.

tasks.title: File Handling and Exceptions
tasks.subtitle: open(), with context manager, try/except/finally & custom errors
tasks.overview: Interact with the file system safely. Learn how to open, read, write, and append files using the with context manager, and handle runtime errors gracefully with try/except blocks.

lesson.heading: The with Statement & Safe File Access
lesson.body: Always use the with context manager when opening files: with open('data.txt', 'r') as file:. Python guarantees the file descriptor is closed automatically, even if an exception occurs.

lesson.heading: Reading and Writing Modes
lesson.body:
- 'r': read mode (default; raises FileNotFoundError if missing)
- 'w': write mode (truncates existing file or creates new)
- 'a': append mode (appends to end of file)
- 'r+': read and write

lesson.heading: Handling Errors with try/except/finally
lesson.body: Wrap risky operations in a try block. Catch specific exceptions: except FileNotFoundError: or except ValueError: rather than catching bare Exception. The optional finally block always runs.

examples.title: Safely catching file missing errors
examples.explanation: The try/except structure catches the missing file error without crashing the application.

practicals.prompt: Which file open mode overwrites an existing file from the beginning?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Mode 'w' truncates the file if it exists or creates a new one.

practicals.prompt: Does the 'finally' block in a try/except structure run even if an exception occurred?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! The 'finally' block is guaranteed to execute regardless of whether an exception occurred.

practicals.prompt: Write a try/except block that catches ZeroDivisionError when dividing 10 by 0, and prints "Cannot divide by zero".

tasks.title: Modules, Packages, Pip, Virtual Environments
tasks.subtitle: import, __name__, standard library, pip & venv isolation
tasks.overview: Structure larger Python projects. Master import statements, explore Python's rich standard library, inspect __name__ == '__main__', and isolate third-party packages with venv and pip.

lesson.heading: Modules and the import Statement
lesson.body: Every Python source file is a module. Use import math or from datetime import datetime to incorporate existing code. Python avoids re-importing already loaded modules.

lesson.heading: The __name__ == '__main__' Pattern
lesson.body: When a Python file is run directly, its special __name__ variable is set to '__main__'. When imported by another file, __name__ matches the module name. This lets you write code that only executes when run as a standalone script.

lesson.heading: Pip and Virtual Environments (venv)
lesson.body: Pip is Python's official package manager. Virtual environments (python -m venv .venv) isolate project dependencies so different apps on the same machine never conflict.

examples.title: Importing math and using functions
examples.code:
import math
print(math.isqrt(49))
examples.explanation: math.isqrt calculates the integer square root cleanly.

practicals.prompt: Is pip the standard package installer for Python libraries?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! pip comes bundled with modern Python installations.

practicals.prompt: What command creates a local virtual environment named 'env'?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! python -m venv <directory> is the built-in command to initialize an isolated environment.

practicals.prompt: Import the math module and print math.ceil(4.2).
practicals.aiExplanation: Great! math.ceil rounds a decimal upward to the nearest integer.

tasks.overview: Model real-world entities with classes. Master the constructor __init__, understand the explicit self parameter, build instance methods, and create hierarchical class structures using inheritance.

lesson.heading: Classes and Objects
lesson.body: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. An object is an instance of a class that bundles state (attributes) and behavior (methods) together.

lesson.heading: The __init__ Constructor and self
lesson.body: When a new instance is created, Python automatically invokes the __init__ initializer method. The first parameter, self, explicitly refers to the specific instance being created or operated on.

lesson.heading: Inheritance and super()
lesson.body: Inheritance allows a subclass to inherit attributes and methods from a parent class: class Dog(Animal):. Use super().__init__() to call the parent class initializer.

examples.title: Defining a simple BankAccount class
examples.explanation: acct maintains its own balance attribute and modifies it through the deposit method.

practicals.prompt: What is the conventional name of the first parameter in an instance method?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Python explicitly passes the instance as the first argument, conventionally named 'self'.

practicals.prompt: Can a class inherit from another class in Python?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! Python supports single and multiple inheritance.

practicals.prompt: Create a class Car with attribute model set in __init__. Instantiate Car("Sedan") and print its model.
practicals.aiExplanation: Well done! Instance attributes are bound to self inside __init__.

tasks.title: Comprehensions, Lambda, Iterators, Generators
tasks.subtitle: List/dict comprehensions, anonymous functions & lazy evaluation with yield
tasks.overview: Write elegant, idiomatic Python. Master concise list and dict comprehensions, lightweight lambda expressions, the iterator protocol (iter/next), and memory-efficient generators using yield.

lesson.heading: List and Dict Comprehensions
lesson.body: Comprehensions provide a concise way to create new collections from existing iterables: [x * 2 for x in numbers if x > 0]. They are faster and more readable than manual loops.

lesson.heading: Lambda Functions
lesson.body: A lambda function is an anonymous inline function defined with lambda args: expression. Use them for short callbacks, like sorting: sorted(items, key=lambda x: x['price']).

lesson.heading: Generators and yield
lesson.body: Generators produce items on demand (lazy evaluation) rather than storing all elements in memory. A function that contains the 'yield' keyword becomes a generator factory.

examples.title: List comprehension filtering evens
examples.code:
evens = [x for x in range(1, 7) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)
examples.explanation: The comprehension filters elements that satisfy x % 2 == 0.

practicals.prompt: Does a generator using 'yield' compute and store all values in RAM immediately?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Generators produce values lazily one at a time on demand.

practicals.prompt: Which comprehension syntax creates a list of squared numbers from 1 to 3?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Square brackets produce a list comprehension.

practicals.prompt: Create a list comprehension that doubles each item in [1, 2, 3] and prints the resulting list.
practicals.aiExplanation: Nice work! [x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3]] transforms the collection cleanly.

tasks.title: JSON, CSV, Dates, Regex
tasks.subtitle: json.loads/dumps, csv.reader/writer, datetime arithmetic & re regex
tasks.overview: Process standard data interchange formats. Parse and serialize JSON payloads, read and write tabular CSV files, calculate date differences with datetime, and validate text patterns with regex (re).

lesson.heading: Working with JSON
lesson.body: Python's json module serializes dictionaries to JSON text with json.dumps() and parses JSON text into Python dictionaries with json.loads(). For files, use json.dump() and json.load().

lesson.heading: Tabular CSV Data
lesson.body: The csv module provides csv.reader and csv.DictReader to process comma-separated values row by row, automatically handling quoted fields.

lesson.heading: Datetime & Timestamps
lesson.body: From the datetime module, datetime.now() gives the current timestamp, and timedelta represents a duration. Formatting is done via .strftime("%Y-%m-%d").

lesson.heading: Pattern Matching with Regex (re)
lesson.body: The re module enables regular expression searches and validations: re.search(r'\d+', text) finds numbers, and re.findall() collects all matches.

examples.title: Parsing JSON text to a Python dictionary
examples.code:
import json
payload = '{"service": "api", "status": 200}'
data = json.loads(payload)
print(data["service"], data["status"])
examples.explanation: json.loads parses the JSON string into an accessible Python dictionary.

practicals.prompt: Which json function parses a JSON string into a Python dictionary?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! json.loads() loads from a string, while json.load() loads from a file object.

practicals.prompt: Does the re module come built-in with standard Python installations?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! The regular expression module 're' is part of the Python standard library.

practicals.prompt: Import json, serialize d = {"active": True} using json.dumps(d), and print the JSON string.
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! json.dumps converts Python's True into JSON's lowercase true.

lesson.heading: Function Decorators and @ Syntax
lesson.body: A decorator is a callable that takes a function as an argument and returns an augmented wrapper function. Decorators cleanly add cross-cutting concerns like logging, timing, and authentication.

lesson.heading: Custom Context Managers
lesson.body: Classes that implement __enter__() and __exit__() can be used with the 'with' statement. Alternatively, contextlib.contextmanager provides a generator-based shortcut.

lesson.heading: Type Hints and Static Typing
lesson.body: Python 3 supports type hints: def query(name: str, limit: int = 10) -> list[str]:. Type hints document code intent and allow static type checkers like mypy to catch bugs before execution.

examples.title: A basic logging decorator
examples.explanation: The @announce decorator intercepts the call, prints the announcement, and executes ping.

practicals.prompt: Do Python type hints enforce runtime type restrictions by default?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Type hints are ignored by the Python interpreter at runtime; they are used by linters and IDEs.

practicals.prompt: Which symbol is used above a function definition to apply a decorator?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! The @decorator syntax is Python's decorator application symbol.

practicals.prompt: Write a typed function greet(name: str) -> str that returns f"Hi, {name}". Call and print greet("Sam").
practicals.aiExplanation: Great! You defined a typed function with annotations and returned the expected greeting.

lesson.heading: Unit Testing with Assertions & pytest
lesson.body: Automated tests verify that your functions behave according to contract. In pytest, simply write functions starting with test_ and use standard assert statements: assert calculate_tax(100) == 10.

lesson.heading: Interactive Debugging with breakpoint()
lesson.body: Python 3.7+ includes built-in breakpoint(), which drops execution straight into the pdb debugger. Inspect local variables, step through lines, and evaluate expressions live.

lesson.heading: Structured Logging
lesson.body: The logging module provides standardized logging levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. Logging includes timestamps, module origin, and can output to both console and files simultaneously.

examples.title: A standard test assertion
examples.explanation: The assert statement succeeds silently when True, confirming expected behavior.

practicals.prompt: Which logging level represents a critical problem that may halt the program?

practicals.prompt: Does an 'assert False' statement raise an AssertionError?

practicals.prompt: Write a test that asserts 5 + 5 == 10, then prints "Assertions verified".

lesson.heading: PEP 8 Style Guide Principles
lesson.body:
PEP 8 is the official Python style guide. Key conventions include:
- 4 spaces per indentation level (never tabs)
- snake_case for functions and variables
- PascalCase for class names
- UPPER_CASE for constants
- Imports grouped at the top of the file

lesson.heading: Linters and Formatters
lesson.body: Modern teams use tools like Black (uncompromising code formatter) and Flake8/Ruff (linter) to enforce consistent formatting across repositories automatically.

lesson.heading: Essential Git Workflow
lesson.body:
Git tracks historical changes:
- git status: inspect modified files
- git add & git commit -m: record a milestone
- git branch & git checkout -b: create isolated feature branches
- git merge / pull request: integrate changes

examples.title: PEP 8 compliant naming and structure
examples.explanation: Constant in UPPER_CASE, class in PascalCase, and methods in snake_case follow PEP 8.

practicals.prompt: According to PEP 8, what naming convention should be used for function names?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Functions and variable names in Python should use lowercase words separated by underscores.

practicals.prompt: Does PEP 8 recommend using 4 spaces per indentation level?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! 4 spaces is the standard indentation recommended by PEP 8.

practicals.prompt: Declare a PEP 8 compliant constant APP_VERSION = "2.1" and print it.

tasks.title: Databases (SQLite/SQL), APIs, Web Scraping
tasks.subtitle: sqlite3 CRUD queries, requests REST endpoints & BeautifulSoup parsing
tasks.overview: Connect Python to the outside data universe. Store structured records in SQLite relational databases, consume REST APIs over HTTP, and extract content from web pages using BeautifulSoup.

lesson.heading: Embedded Relational Databases with sqlite3
lesson.body: Python includes sqlite3 built-in. Connect with sqlite3.connect('app.db'), create a cursor, and execute parameterized SQL queries to avoid SQL injection: cursor.execute('INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)', (name, email)).

lesson.heading: Consuming REST APIs
lesson.body: The requests library (or urllib) performs HTTP GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE operations. Check response.status_code and parse JSON payloads with response.json().

lesson.heading: HTML Parsing and Web Scraping
lesson.body: Libraries like BeautifulSoup (bs4) parse HTML markup, allowing you to query elements by tags, classes, or CSS selectors to extract text, tables, and links.

examples.title: In-memory SQLite database operations
examples.code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE items (name TEXT, qty INT)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES ('Apples', 10)")
conn.commit()

cur.execute("SELECT name, qty FROM items")
row = cur.fetchone()
print(f"{row[0]}: {row[1]}")
conn.close()
examples.explanation: Creates an in-memory database, inserts a row, queries it back, and closes the connection cleanly.

practicals.prompt: What HTTP status code indicates a successful request?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! HTTP 200 OK signals that the request succeeded.

practicals.prompt: Should you format variables directly into SQL strings using f-strings instead of parameterized queries?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! Direct string formatting in SQL introduces SQL injection vulnerabilities; always use parameterized placeholders (?).

practicals.prompt: Import sqlite3, connect to ':memory:', create a cursor, and print "Connected to SQLite".
practicals.aiExplanation: Nice work! sqlite3 is built right into the Python standard library.

tasks.title: Concurrency: Threads, Multiprocessing, Asyncio
tasks.subtitle: GIL, threading, multiprocessing pools & async/await event loops
tasks.overview: Execute workloads concurrently. Understand Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), choose between I/O-bound threading, CPU-bound multiprocessing, and modern non-blocking asynchronous programming with asyncio.

lesson.heading: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
lesson.body: CPython uses a mutex called the GIL to ensure only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Consequently, threading works well for I/O-bound tasks (network/disk waits), but does not speed up CPU-bound math.

lesson.heading: Multiprocessing for CPU Workloads
lesson.body: The multiprocessing module bypasses the GIL by spawning distinct operating system processes, each with its own Python interpreter and memory space, utilizing multi-core processors effectively.

lesson.heading: Asynchronous I/O with asyncio
lesson.body: asyncio provides single-threaded cooperative multitasking using an event loop. Define coroutines with async def and pause them cooperatively with await to handle thousands of concurrent network connections without thread overhead.

examples.title: A basic asyncio coroutine
examples.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch_data():
    return "Payload received"

async def main():
    result = await fetch_data()
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())
examples.explanation: async def creates a coroutine, and asyncio.run executes it inside an event loop.

practicals.prompt: Which concurrency model is optimal for CPU-heavy tasks on multi-core machines in Python?
practicals.aiExplanation: Correct! multiprocessing spawns separate processes, each bypassing the GIL to use independent CPU cores.

practicals.prompt: Can a coroutine declared with 'async def' use the 'await' keyword inside its body?
practicals.aiExplanation: Spot on! Coroutines defined with 'async def' use 'await' to yield control to the event loop.

practicals.prompt: Import asyncio, define async def main() returning "Async OK", run it with asyncio.run(main()), and print the result.
practicals.aiExplanation: Great! asyncio.run handles the event loop lifecycle cleanly.

lesson.heading: Production Best Practices
